title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id: cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates the effect of downstream deterministic tooling (a NetOps verifier + lightweight topology simulator) on validator pass/fail outcomes when the same single LLM candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks (600 episodes); completed: 598 episodes → 299 complete pairs. Deterministic validator outcomes: baseline 299/299 pass; guarded (tool‑augmented post‑processing) 299/299 pass (contingency n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). The run used gpt-5-mini (declared) and a recorded deterministic validator; all raw responses, validator traces, provider traces, and execution logs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest. Because the design fixes generation (shared candidate), these results answer the narrow question of whether downstream verifier/simulator processing changes pass/fail for identical candidates; they do not address whether independent tool‑augmented agentic generation would produce different or safer candidates. We report execution accounting, a concise failure post‑mortem for the missing pair, and concrete methodological lessons for future independent‑generation evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation is operationally critical but risky because misconfigurations cause outages and security failures. Recent architectures pair generative LLMs with deterministic validators, simulators, and repair loops to reduce that risk. Prior empirical work often conflates generator improvements with downstream tooling effects. We designed a confirmatory, preregistered paired experiment whose purpose is narrowly stated and frozen a priori: given an identical LLM candidate for both arms (shared_initial_candidate), does downstream tool‑augmentation (deterministic verifier + lightweight simulator applied as post‑processing) change deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes? This choice removes generator variance and isolates post‑generation tooling effects. We report a fully archived run (preregistration: cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1), exact accounting, and the definitive artifact‑grounded outcome. Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired evaluation isolating verifier/post‑processing effects; (2) exact, reproducible reporting of contingency counts, test statistics, and CI derived from archived scoring JSONs and validator traces; (3) methodological diagnosis of a ceiling effect and prescriptive design guidance for follow‑ups that test independent agentic generation.
sections.related_work: We position this run relative to intent→config and LLM→NetOps work that combines generation with deterministic checks and tool chains (representative leads: intent‑to‑config and LLM translation work [10.1002/nem.2313], PreConfig (arXiv:2403.09369), RAG/agent tool architectures and verifier studies [10.20944/preprints202604.1820.v1]; tool‑augmentation reliability designs and verifier tradeoffs [10.2139/ssrn.7317098, 10.5220/0013221900003890]). Those works motivated our focus on downstream tooling reliability; our design differs by fixing the generator and evaluating only the post‑generation tool chain’s impact on deterministic validation outcomes.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) was frozen before any execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator pass indicator. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided; bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Crucial fixed semantics: shared_initial_candidate — a single LLM generation was produced per task and reused verbatim by both pipelines (baseline and guarded). Rationale: isolate effects of verification/simulation/repair post‑processing on the same candidate. Execution contract and artifacts. Adapter/orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task bank: deterministic synthetic topology templates with explicit initial/final states, per‑task difficulty metadata and workflow constraints; confirmatory sample = 300 paired tasks (150 simple, 150 complex by preregistered strata). Inclusion/exclusion: exact matches to a curated public config corpus would be excluded per preregistration and moved to exploratory; all detections were logged (see execution manifest). Logging and provenance. The run archived all provider calls, raw model outputs, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and execution logs, with full SHA‑256 hashing; authoritative artifact paths and hashes are recorded in the execution manifest and in the manuscript evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting (artifact‑backed). Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes: 598. Failed episodes: 2 (both belong to a single missing pair; pair‑000269). Complete analyzable pairs: 299. Model calls used: 300 (completed calls 299; failed 1). Representative artifact locations (authoritative): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256: 6569b491...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha256: cefa6344...), execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha256: b45a6008...). Confirmatory outcome (archival counts). Contingency for complete pairs (n=299): n11 = 299 (both pass), n10 = 0 (guarded pass & baseline fail), n01 = 0 (baseline pass & guarded fail), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline successes = 299/299 (100.0%). Guarded successes = 299/299 (100.0%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Missingness and failure post‑mortem (artifact citations). The single excluded pair is pair‑000269; two failed episodes produced one missing pair. The execution log contains the provider error and timestamp entries; authoritative log path: execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8). Short post‑mortem: the provider call for the shared_initial generation for that pair returned a transient API error (provider error code and timestamp appear in execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json; the call was recorded as failed and the pair excluded per the preregistered missingness plan). All failure records, provider error codes, and call hashes are archived in execution/provider_calls/* and the execution log; no manual substitution or re‑generation was performed.
sections.discussion: What the observed result means. Under the executed semantics (shared_initial_candidate), downstream tool‑augmentation (validator + simulator post‑processing) did not change deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes for the identical LLM candidates in our confirmatory set: both arms accepted the same candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs. This is a narrowly stated, artifact‑grounded factual result and should not be generalized beyond the executed estimand. Ceiling effect and power ramifications. The preregistration powered the test assuming baseline pass ≈ 0.60 and targeted detecting a +0.20 absolute paired improvement with n=300. The observed baseline pass = 1.00 (299/299) violates that assumption and produces a ceiling effect: the preregistered minimally important effect is unobservable in this dataset. We therefore report exact contingency counts, the exact McNemar p‑value, and bootstrap CI rather than claim a powered null. Design lessons and next steps. To test whether an agentic tool‑augmented generator improves safety relative to an LLM‑only baseline, a future preregistration should (a) use independent per‑condition generation semantics (not shared candidate reuse), (b) use a task pool with higher difficulty or adversarial cases to avoid ceiling success rates, and (c) consider multi‑model replication. Operational value of deterministic validators. Even when generator candidates are high quality, deterministic validator traces provide auditable parsing, per‑command validation, and explicit violation codes (useful for deployment audits). Limitations (artifact‑backed): synthetic tasks and a lightweight simulator limit external validity to vendor CLIs and production telemetry; a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) limits generality; validator rule sets capture many, but not all, platform idiosyncrasies.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation that isolates the downstream tooling effect on identical LLM candidates (shared_initial_candidate semantics). For 299 analyzable pairs the archived, reproducible outcome is exact: both arms accepted the same candidates (n11=299). The run is fully archived (responses, validator traces, provider traces, execution logs and SHA‑256 hashes). Because the design fixes generation, these results do not answer whether independent agentic, tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs; that remains a separate estimand requiring a different preregistration. We supply artifact‑anchored execution accounting, a concise failure post‑mortem for the missing pair (pair‑000269) referencing execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha256: b45a6008...), and concrete recommendations for follow‑up confirmatory designs that test independent generation semantics and avoid ceiling effects.

disclosure_statement: This manuscript and all reported results were produced by an autonomous post‑lock research run governed by the immutable master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The preregistration cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 was frozen prior to execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Declared LLM used in the run: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; recorded artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Generation semantics fixed by preregistration: shared_initial_candidate — for each paired task a single LLM candidate was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines; this choice is central to the executed estimand and is specified in the preregistration and execution manifest. Tools permitted under the execution contract: deterministic validator and a lightweight topology simulator; one repair call per task allowed under the frozen retry policy. Execution accounting (authoritative) and artifact bundles: planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (forming one missing pair, pair-000269); complete analyzable pairs = 299. All raw model outputs, provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*), validator traces and scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*), task manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), the execution log (execution/execution_log.jsonl; sha256 b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8), and a full manifest of SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived and are the authoritative source for every reported number. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numeric claims are grounded in these archived execution and analysis artifacts. The run answered the narrowly preregistered estimand (effect of downstream tooling on identical LLM candidates) and did not perform an independent per‑condition agentic generation comparison; any claim beyond the executed estimand would be unsupported by the archived artifacts.
limitations: Executed semantics were shared_initial_candidate (single LLM generation reused across both conditions); the result therefore answers whether post‑generation tooling changes deterministic validator pass/fail for identical candidates, not whether independent agentic, tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Task bank used deterministic synthetic topology templates and a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor CLIs, production telemetry, or richer runtime heterogeneity is limited.
Only a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a specified rule set (workflow/dependency patterns such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break); it cannot exhaustively model all platform or hardware idiosyncrasies.

A ceiling effect occurred: observed baseline success (299/299) violated the preregistered power assumption and makes the originally targeted minimally important effect (pre‑registered +0.20 absolute paired difference) unobservable in this execution.
